title: A Startup Has a Plan to Make Water From Air Using Data Centers’ Waste Heat
gist: Irvine startup Atoco uses metal organic frameworks, the Nobel-winning materials from founder Omar Yaghi, to harvest water from air using only low-grade heat, and is pitching them to AI data centers that emit waste heat and consume huge amounts of water. A prototype makes up to 300 liters per day at roughly $5 per ton, but scaling to hyperscale demand and beating newer desalination at $2 per ton remain unproven.

insights.claim: Atoco's metal organic frameworks, which won founder Omar Yaghi the 2025 chemistry Nobel, harvest water from air without grid power, requiring only low-level heat to release it.
insights.speaker: Brian Kahn
insights.so_what: A commercial path for Nobel-grade materials science into water supply.

insights.claim: MOFs act like molecular sponges with a jungle-gym structure; a gram can cover two football fields of surface and can store hydrogen, CO2 or water.
insights.speaker: Omar Yaghi
insights.so_what: The same material platform spans clean energy, carbon capture and water.

insights.claim: Atoco's system works at relative humidity in the teens and releases water with heat as low as 100 degrees Fahrenheit, outperforming silica desiccants that need much more heat.
insights.speaker: Brian Kahn
insights.so_what: Low regeneration temperature is what makes waste-heat integration plausible.
insights.locator: The monolith in the parking lot

insights.claim: Roughly 70 percent of industrial waste heat is low-grade and unused, which Atoco says could yield trillions of liters of clean water.
insights.speaker: Samer Taha
insights.so_what: Waste heat is a large untapped input if the technology scales.
insights.quote: Roughly 70 percent of the industrial waste heat is low-grade, unutilized, thrown into oceans or into the air

insights.claim: Atoco's CEO says the AI data center buildout was not on its radar four or five years ago but created an opening, since data centers produce abundant waste heat and need lots of water.
insights.speaker: Samer Taha
insights.so_what: AI infrastructure growth is creating demand for adjacent water and cooling solutions.
insights.quote: We were not really thinking of AI data centers
insights.locator: “We were not really thinking of AI data centers,” four or five years ago

insights.claim: Data centers can emit heat equal to tens of thousands of homes and some cooling systems consume millions of gallons per day; Atoco claims to tackle both problems by turning heat into water.
insights.speaker: Brian Kahn
insights.so_what: Water and heat constraints are growing siting and cost issues for AI data centers.
insights.locator: Data centers are an increasingly big source

insights.claim: Microsoft, Google and Amazon Web Services have committed to being water positive by 2030, which signals a potential market for water-from-heat technology.
insights.speaker: Brian Kahn
insights.so_what: Corporate water pledges create demand for solutions like Atoco's.
insights.locator: But there are signs that there could be a market

insights.claim: The parking-lot demo makes up to 300 liters per day on heat equivalent to a 20-kilowatt data center; a commercial product targets up to 1,000 liters daily, versus hyperscale data centers that are orders of magnitude bigger.
insights.speaker: Brian Kahn
insights.so_what: Large gap between current output and data center needs is the main scale risk.
insights.locator: To do that, let alone serve data centers

insights.claim: Atoco has run five on-grid prototype trials in the US and Gulf Cooperation Council, hopes to take first product orders by year-end, and is in talks with unnamed major tech companies about pilots.
insights.speaker: Brian Kahn
insights.so_what: Watch for first orders and a named data center pilot as validation.
insights.locator: Atoco has deployed five on-grid prototype trials

insights.claim: Atoco's levelized water cost is $5 per metric ton, competitive with older desalination, while newer plants deliver at $2 per ton or less, a target Atoco says is three to five years away.
insights.speaker: Samer Taha
insights.so_what: Cost must fall further to compete broadly with modern desalination.
insights.locator: Taha says the company can produce water

insights.claim: MOFs are not a silver bullet: without outside heat they still need energy to release water, which makes rural deployment hard, and the technology is untested at scale.
